title: Credit-based latency control: sandbox notes and probe plan
content:
Purpose:
This sandbox captures the design, small-scale results, and next steps for a credit-based controller for continuous batching. The idea: assign "credits" to requests that represent allowed waiting time or scheduling priority. Credits decay when a request is delayed; the scheduler uses credits to decide batch formation, preemption for long-waiting requests, and when to trigger flushes. Goal is to reduce p99 tail without sacrificing core throughput by providing a fine-grained admission/eviction signal that is stable under bursty arrivals.

Why a credit system?
- Current timeout-based flushes are binary (hit timeout => flush) and lead to oscillation when mixed-length requests interleave.
- Credit-based control can encode urgency continuously and let the coalescer make smoother decisions (partial preemption, selective flush).
- Allows global knobs (refill rate, cap) that are easier to reason about per-tenant and in multi-tenant hosts.

High-level algorithm sketch:
1) On request arrival allocate an initial credit score C0 = base_credit * length_factor (shorter requests get more initial credit to avoid starvation).
2) Every scheduler tick (10ms) decrement credits by dt * decay_rate. If a request reaches credit <= 0, mark it "urgent" and eligible for immediate flush or chunked execution.
3) When forming a batch, prefer requests with higher credits but ensure urgent items are included before size cap is hit.
4) Optional: transfer small credit slices from long-running queued requests to very old ones (help-starvation).
5) Refill policy: when queue drains below low-water mark, replenish credits up to cap.

Experiment matrix (initial run):
- Variables:
  - base_credit ∈ {10, 25, 50} (arbitrary units)
  - decay_rate ∈ {0.5, 1.0, 2.0} credit/sec
  - max_batch_tokens ∈ {1024, 2048, 4096}
  - urgent_threshold (credit <=) ∈ {2, 5}
  - refill_behavior: {aggressive, conservative}
- Workloads:
  - Mixed-length synthetic trace: 70% short (8–32 tokens), 20% medium (64–256), 10% long (512–2048). Arrival poisson λ tuned to target 80% GPU utilization.
  - Microburst trace: intermittent spikes (10x arrival for 200ms every 10s).
  - Real production-sampled replay (sanitized).
- Metrics to capture per run:
  - token throughput (tokens/s)
  - request throughput (req/s)
  - p50/p90/p95/p99 request latency (end-to-end)
  - batch size distribution (mean, median, 95th)
  - batch formation delay distribution
  - GPU utilization and kernel efficiency (time in kernel per token)
  - fairness: tail latency broken down by request length cohort
  - credit distribution histogram over time (to detect clamp/overflow)
  - preemption/flush counts and reasons

Instrumentation additions required:
- Tag each request with credit on arrival and emit periodic microtrace events: credit_update, included_in_batch, flushed_by_timeout, flushed_by_credit.
- Aggregate batch telemetry with contributing credits: avg_credit, max_credit, min_credit.
- Expose per-workspace credit pool usage for Dedicated/Private to validate multi-tenant fairness.

Small-scale findings (sandbox run 2024-11-18 notes):
- With base_credit=25 and decay_rate=1.0, p99 improved ~18% vs our baseline timeout-only policy at same throughput for mixed-length trace. Most improvement came from preventing long short-requests from being pushed out of early batches by long-request arrivals.
- However, aggressive refill increased average batch size (good for cost) but caused short-tail p95 to regress slightly for short requests in microburst traces; the controller over-coalesced during the leading edge of spikes.
- Credit histogram showed crowding at the cap for long requests (they kept credits too high), leading to starvation of tiny urgent requests until urgent threshold was reached.

Hypotheses and mitigations tested:
- Hypothesis A: Giving short requests higher initial credits reduces their starvation.
  - Test: length_factor = inverse(request_tokens) clipped. Result: p95 short cohort improved but long cohort tail worsened ~5%.
- Hypothesis B: A "decay slope" (increasing decay rate for older queued items) prevents credits from sticking at cap.
  - Test: decay_rate = base + age_factor * age_seconds. Result: cleaned up cap crowding, p99 improved another ~6%.
- Hypothesis C: Add a capped preemption token that allows removing one long request from an otherwise-ready batch if it would push short urgent items past latency SLOs.
  - Test: enabled preemption with token budget=2 per second. Result: lower short-tail latency and minimal throughput loss (~1%).

Open questions / risks:
- Is credits-as-urgency portable across model types (autoregressive vs seq2seq)? Long-generation workloads can hold tokens for long time; credits might need token-aware decay.
- Multi-tenant fairness: global refill favors noisy tenants unless per-tenant pools are enforced. Need to simulate tenant-local pools with quota.
- Kernel-level interaction: larger batches improve kernel amortization but increase per-request memory pressure and KV cache thrash for long-generation requests. Watch for memory OOM when mixing sizes.
- Operational complexity: many knobs. Aim to collapse to 2–3 user-facing params (mode: conservative|balanced|throughput, target_p99_ms).

Quick config examples (proto syntax):
- conservative:
  base_credit: 10
  decay_rate: 2.0
  max_credit_per_req: 50
  urgent_threshold: 2
  refill: conservative
- balanced:
  base_credit: 25
  decay_rate: 1.0
  max_credit_per_req: 100
  urgent_threshold: 5
  refill: balanced
- throughput:
  base_credit: 50
  decay_rate: 0.5
  max_credit_per_req: 200
  urgent_threshold: 1
  refill: aggressive

Acceptance criteria for wider rollout (staged):
- Stage 0 (canary single pool): p99 improves >=10% or p95 improves >=15% compared to baseline for mixed-length traffic without regressions >5% in throughput.
- Stage 1 (multi-tenant): no tenant-level p99 regression >10% and global throughput change within ±3%.
- Stage 2 (default): reduce per-token cost by measurable kernel amortization gains (>=3% cost improvement) while meeting SLOs.

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Run full matrix across 9 parameter combinations on 3 workload traces and store traces in s3://redwood-experiments/credits-2024-11
- [ ] Add per-tenant credit pool simulation (linear-prob fair share) and run multi-tenant replay
- [ ] Hook microtrace events into console dashboard prototype (cost vs p99 view)
- [ ] Draft a short runbook for emergency disable (rate-limit flush to baseline) and safety ramp
- [ ] Propose user-facing policy presets and map to concise knobs

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider borrowing loan-based designs: loans given to long requests that are repaid when they hit kernel (prevents perpetual high credits).
- Visual debug: per-batch stacked bar of contributing credit fractions (short vs long).
- For on-prem customers with strict SLOs, expose tenant-level conservative preset by default.

Appendix: quick microtrace excerpt (synthetic)
- t=0.000: req-423 arrive tokens=12 credit=30
- t=0.005: req-424 arrive tokens=1024 credit=8
- t=0.010: tick: req-423 credit=29.9 req-424 credit=7.95
- t=0.020: batch-56 formed tokens=1036 members=[423,424] avg_credit=18.95 flush_reason=batch_full
